examples.knowledge_point: Improper Integrals Involving Arctangent Using the Second Result
examples.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the following result:

$$
\int \dfrac{1}{k^2 + x^2} \, \textrm dx = \dfrac{1}{k} \arctan \left( \dfrac{x}{k} \right) + C
$$

We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to\infty.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2\sqrt{3}}^{\infty }\frac{6}{{x}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}x & =6\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{2\sqrt{3}}^{a}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =6\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{2\sqrt{3}}^{a}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{2}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =6\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{2})]}_{2\sqrt{3}}^{a} \\  & =3{lim}_{a\to \infty }(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{a}{2})-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\sqrt{3})) \\  & =3{lim}_{a\to \infty }(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{a}{2})-\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =3{lim}_{a\to \infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{a}{2})]-\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y=\arctan\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right),$ shown in the graph below:

- $\lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} \left[\arctan\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)\right] = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}$

- $\lim\limits_{x \to \infty} \left[\arctan\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)\right] = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14039465/assets/042ad2450306552d9d5a7e4219d15547ad7104601b7ce6350a64193981de0de7.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2\sqrt{3}}^{\infty }\frac{6}{{x}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}x & =3{lim}_{a\to \infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{a}{2})]-\pi  \\  & =3\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}-\pi  \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the following result:

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+(kx)^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{k}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(kx)+C
$$

We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\sqrt{3}/9}^{\infty }\frac{15}{9{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x & =15\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{\sqrt{3}/9}^{a}\frac{1}{9{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =15\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{\sqrt{3}/9}^{a}\frac{1}{(3x)^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =15\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(3x)]}_{\sqrt{3}/9}^{a} \\  & =5\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(3a)-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3})) \\  & =5\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }\operatorname{arctan}⁡(3a)-\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =5\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }\operatorname{arctan}⁡(3a)-\frac{5\pi }{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(3x),$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }\operatorname{arctan}⁡(3x)=-\frac{\pi }{2}$

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }\operatorname{arctan}⁡(3x)=\frac{\pi }{2}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14039465/assets/9f882cb5102270dfe4bef256782c18aaeeca3518f564cd188298040237e30f62.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\sqrt{3}/9}^{\infty }\frac{15}{9{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x & =5\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }\operatorname{arctan}⁡(3a)-\frac{5\pi }{6} \\  & =5\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}-\frac{5\pi }{6} \\  & =\frac{5\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
